questions.question: 1. What is the main difference between a point operation and a neighbourhood operation?

answers.a: A neighbourhood operation uses information from surrounding pixels
answers.b: A neighbourhood operation can be applied only to colour images
answers.c: A point operation always changes the image dimensions
answers.d: A point operation requires a filter matrix

explanations.a: Correct. A neighbourhood operation computes an output pixel using a local neighbourhood, whereas a point operation uses the corresponding input pixel.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The distinction between the two operations is based on how pixel information is used, not on whether the image is colour or grayscale.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Point operations do not inherently change the image dimensions.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A filter matrix is used for linear neighbourhood operations, but it is not a requirement of point operations.

questions.question: 2. Which of the following is a linear neighbourhood operation discussed in the experiment?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The experiment classifies the median filter as a nonlinear neighbourhood operation.
explanations.b: Correct. Gaussian filtering is presented as a linear filtering operation using filter coefficients in a convolution.
explanations.c: Incorrect. File conversion is not a neighbourhood operation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Pixel threshold selection is not the linear filtering operation described in the experiment.

questions.question: 3. Which filter is described as a nonlinear neighbourhood operation in the experiment?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The straight averaging filter is presented as a linear filter.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The triangular filter is presented among the linear filters.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The Gaussian filter is presented as a linear filter.
explanations.d: Correct. The median filter is a nonlinear operation because it uses a ranking operation on the neighbourhood values.

questions.question: 4. For a $3 \times 3$ averaging filter, each coefficient is equal and the coefficients sum to $1$. What is the value of each coefficient?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Nine equal coefficients with this value would make their total greater than $1$.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Nine equal coefficients with this value would not sum to $1$.
explanations.c: Correct. There are nine equal coefficients, so each coefficient is $\frac{1}{9}$ to make their sum equal to $1$.
explanations.d: Incorrect. If every one of the nine coefficients were $1$, their sum would not be $1$.

questions.question: 5. An image contains isolated black and white pixels caused by salt-and-pepper noise. Which operation described in the experiment is particularly useful for removing this type of noise?

explanations.a: Correct. The experiment describes median filtering as a nonlinear operation that can effectively remove isolated salt-and-pepper noise.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The experiment does not identify the triangular filter as the specific nonlinear operation used to remove salt-and-pepper noise.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Changing image dimensions does not by itself remove isolated noisy pixels.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Changing the file format does not perform the neighbourhood filtering needed to remove this noise.

questions.question: 6. In a linear neighbourhood operation, what is the role of the centre coefficient $w(0,0)$?

answers.b: It is the coefficient applied at the position of the current pixel
answers.c: It specifies the number of image channels
answers.d: It determines the border size automatically

explanations.a: Incorrect. Image width is not represented by the centre coefficient of a filter.
explanations.b: Correct. $w(0,0)$ is the coefficient at the centre of the window, corresponding to the position of the current pixel.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The number of image channels is unrelated to the centre coefficient of the filter.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The centre coefficient does not by itself determine how image borders are handled.

questions.question: 7. A $3 \times 3$ neighbourhood window is applied to a pixel at the border of an image. What problem occurs if no border-handling method is used?

answers.a: Some pixels required by the window are outside the image
answers.c: The centre pixel is removed from the image

explanations.a: Correct. Part of the $3 \times 3$ neighbourhood can lie outside the image at a border, so the required input values are unavailable.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The filter coefficients do not change sign merely because the window reaches an image border.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Border handling concerns unavailable neighbourhood pixels and does not remove the centre pixel.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Reaching an image border does not change a linear filter into a nonlinear operation.

questions.question: 8. Suppose a neighbourhood filter has positive coefficients whose sum is $1$. Which effect is most consistent with the low pass filters described in the experiment?

answers.b: Guaranteed conversion to a binary image
answers.d: Dependence only on the centre pixel

explanations.a: Correct. The experiment describes local averaging or smoothing as a low pass filtering operation with positive coefficients and a coefficient sum of $1$.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Low pass filtering does not imply that the output will be binary.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Smoothing modifies local intensity variations but does not remove all image information.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A neighbourhood filter uses multiple pixels in its local window rather than only the centre pixel.

questions.question: 9. Which statement best distinguishes the Gaussian filter from the median filter as presented in the experiment?

answers.a: The Gaussian filter is nonlinear, while the median filter is linear
answers.b: Both filters use exactly the same type of operation
answers.c: The Gaussian filter uses weighted linear filtering, while the median filter uses a nonlinear ranking operation
answers.d: The Gaussian filter uses only the centre pixel, while the median filter uses the whole image

explanations.a: Incorrect. This reverses the classification of these two filters given in the experiment.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The experiment distinguishes these filters by the different ways they combine neighbourhood pixel values.
explanations.c: Correct. The Gaussian filter is presented as a linear filter using coefficients in a convolution, while the median filter uses a nonlinear ranking operation.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Both operations work on local neighbourhoods; neither is defined in the experiment as using only the centre pixel or the whole image.
